status.en: 14 armed incidents reported in the past seven days, 56% more than the week before, most of them in Caracas, Valencia and Maracaibo.
status.nb: 14 væpnede hendelser meldt de siste sju dagene, 56 prosent flere enn uken før, flest i Caracas, Valencia og Maracaibo.

summary.en: Venezuela is expanding a major military operation in the Apure plains, sending Bolivarian forces across the border to hunt irregular armed groups and destroy their logistics network. The United States is deploying drones to target Colombia’s ELN guerrilla group as Venezuela shifts its stance, and a report suggests a possible US strike on ELN elements inside Venezuela. Lawmakers have opened the crisis-hit power sector to private investment, inviting foreign firms such as Fluor, which has returned after twenty years, and the sector is being opened to private investors. Two battle-related deaths were recorded in 2007, according to UCDP.
summary.nb: Venezuela utvider en stor militæroperasjon på Apure-sletten, og sender bolivariske styrker over grensen for å jakte på irregulære væpnede grupper og ødelegge deres logistikknettverk. USA setter inn droner for å angripe Colombias ELN-gerilja mens Venezuela endrer sin holdning, og en rapport antyder et mulig amerikansk angrep på ELN-elementer inne i Venezuela. Lovgivere har åpnet den kriserammede kraftsektoren for privat investering, og inviterer utenlandske firmaer som Fluor, som har kommet tilbake etter tjue år, og sektoren åpnes for private investorer. To dødsfall i kamper ble registrert i 2007, ifølge UCDP.

background.title: Crisis in Venezuela
background.extract: An ongoing socioeconomic and political crisis began in Venezuela during the presidencies of Hugo Chávez, Nicolás Maduro as well as Delcy Rodríguez. It has been marked by hyperinflation, starvation, disease, crime, and mortality rates, resulting in massive emigration. Food shortages and hyperinflation have ended, but inflation remains high. It is the worst economic crisis in Venezuela's history and considered by some sources as more severe than the Great Depression in the United States, the 1985–1994 Brazilian economic crisis, or the 2008–2009 hyperinflation in Zimbabwe. In 2019, the Institute of International Finance called it the single largest economic collapse outside of war in 45 years. Writers have compared aspects, such as unemployment and GDP contraction, to Bosnia and Herzegovina after the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and those in Russia, Cuba and Albania following the Revolutions of 1989.
